The design decisions: canonical store, view layer, tiered link-quality by chain criticality, and temporal versioning — three matrices (A) would diverge into three conflicting accounts of the same estate, which is precisely what an investigation exploits
options.B: Let each of the three consuming teams — migration, remediation, and the investigation-response function — maintain and use whichever traceability matrix format and structure each team individually prefers, on the reasoning that different consumers naturally have different working styles and tool preferences, and respecting each team's own preferred format avoids the friction of imposing one shared canonical structure across groups with genuinely different day-to-day needs, even though this means the underlying relationship facts could diverge across the three preferred formats over time with no single authoritative account of what the actual shared relationships are, exactly the divergence an investigation could exploit as inconsistency, and treating the burden of reconciling three independently-evolving accounts after the fact — should anyone ever need to compare them — as a manageable future problem rather than as a foreseeable, structural weakness being built into the estate's own design from the very first day the three teams begin working from their own separately preferred formats
options.C: Suspend all traceability maintenance activity entirely for the duration of the open investigation, on the reasoning that any changes made to the trace estate while investigators are actively reviewing related material risk appearing to tamper with or alter records relevant to their inquiry, so the safest course is to freeze all trace-store updates until the investigation formally concludes, even though migration planning and the remediation workstream both continue generating real disposition decisions and evidence chains that need to be traced and recorded throughout this same period regardless of whether the investigation happens to still be open
options.D: Maintain three fully separate traceability matrices, one purpose-built for each of the three consuming needs — migration, remediation, and the investigation — with each matrix independently recording its own version of the underlying requirement relationships according to its own consumer's specific needs, on the reasoning that dedicating an independently structured matrix to each distinct purpose lets each one be optimized precisely for its own consumer without needing to accommodate the others' differing quality standards or view requirements within a single shared structure

questions.explanation:
A. ✓ Correct — one canonical link store with purpose-specific views, tiered link quality by chain criticality, and temporal versioning, since three parallel matrices would diverge into conflicting accounts an investigation could exploit.

B. ✗ Lets three teams maintain their own divergent formats with no canonical shared account of the underlying relationships, creating exactly the kind of inconsistency across parallel records an investigation can exploit.

C. ✗ Halts trace-store maintenance during exactly the period when migration and remediation are generating real disposition decisions and evidence chains that still need recording.

questions.question: The consciously-dropped disposition category (requirements NOT migrating to Meridian's platform) requires governance no one has designed: who can authorize dropping a requirement, and what does dropping mean for its obligations? The expert drop-governance framework distinguishes:

options.A: Drop classes with different authority and residue: (a) obsolete needs (the business condition ended — Product Owner authority, clean drop with rationale); (b) needs Meridian's platform serves DIFFERENTLY (not dropped but transformed — requires equivalence evidence via the scenario method, business-owner sign-off that the different mechanism satisfies the need); (c) needs being consciously unserved going forward (a capability reduction — requires the affected stakeholders' informed acceptance and, where customer-facing or compliance-adjacent, senior authority, because this class is where 'migration' quietly becomes 'service degradation'); (d) compliance-bound requirements (droppable ONLY with Legal's confirmation that the underlying obligation ended — regulator commitments don't expire because platforms change). Each class needs its authority, evidence, and record — undifferentiated drop approval lets class-c and class-d losses hide inside class-a housekeeping
options.B: Establish a policy that no MayOptimize requirement may ever be formally dropped from the estate under any circumstances, regardless of whether the underlying business need has become genuinely obsolete, is being served differently by Meridian's platform, or is being consciously left unserved going forward, on the reasoning that a blanket no-drop policy is the simplest way to guarantee no compliance-bound or customer-facing obligation is ever lost through an improperly authorized drop, even though this means genuinely obsolete, no-longer-relevant requirements accumulate indefinitely in the estate with no path to formal retirement, degrading exactly the signal-to-noise the estate needs to remain useful, on the further reasoning that a single blanket rule requiring board-level engagement is easier to communicate and enforce consistently across a large, unfamiliar combined organization than a differentiated framework whose separate authority levels, evidence standards, and record requirements would need to be explained, trained, and monitored separately for each of the four distinct drop classes the more calibrated approach identifies
options.C: Require that every single requirement drop decision, regardless of whether it concerns a genuinely obsolete internal housekeeping item or a customer-facing compliance-bound obligation, be routed through the same board-level approval process, on the reasoning that uniform board-level scrutiny applied equally to all drop classes guarantees nothing risky ever slips through under a lower authority level, even though this means routine, low-stakes obsolete-need drops consume the same scarce senior-governance attention as genuinely consequential compliance-bound or service-degradation drops, diluting the board's actual attention away from the drop decisions that most need it
options.D: Treat every requirement drop as equivalent to simple deletion requiring one uniform approval step regardless of what kind of need the requirement addressed, on the reasoning that a single, consistent approval gate applied identically to every drop is simpler to administer and audit than a multi-class framework distinguishing different authority levels and evidence requirements for different kinds of drops

questions.explanation:
A. ✓ Correct — distinguish drop classes (obsolete, transformed, unserved, compliance-bound) with escalating authority and evidence, since undifferentiated dropping lets service degradation and compliance breaches masquerade as housekeeping.

B. ✗ Bans all drops outright, letting genuinely obsolete requirements accumulate indefinitely instead of retiring them through the appropriate class-a authority, degrading the estate's own usefulness.

C. ✗ Routes every drop through the same board-level scrutiny regardless of stakes, diluting senior attention away from the genuinely consequential compliance-bound and service-degradation drops that most need it.

D. ✗ Applies one uniform approval gate to every drop class, letting service degradation and compliance breaches masquerade as routine housekeeping.

questions.question: The investigation requests 'all versions of requirement CR-005 and records of who changed it, when, and why, from inception.' The lifecycle records can answer this fully — EXCEPT a 6-week gap in 2024 when a tool migration lost change-comment history (the versions survive; the why-comments don't). The expert disclosure posture on known record gaps is:

options.A: Disclose the gap proactively with its documented cause: counsel-guided disclosure that the change-comment layer for the specified window was lost in a documented tool migration (the migration's own records — dates, incident tickets, what was and wasn't recovered — become the gap's provenance evidence), accompanied by reconstruction where possible (CCB minutes and email records partially cover the missing why-layer) — because discovered-rather-than-disclosed gaps convert a benign technical loss into apparent concealment (investigators finding the hole themselves will ask why it wasn't mentioned), while proactive disclosure with provenance turns the gap into a documented artifact with an innocent explanation. options.D: Approve Meridian's proposed requirements-rationalization approach as presented, treating deduplication via automated text-similarity matching as an unambiguously good hygiene practice that should proceed largely as designed, on the reasoning that reducing a combined 1,440-requirement estate down to its genuinely unique content is self-evidently valuable, without separately examining whether textually similar requirement pairs might actually encode materially different obligations, or whether the merge process as designed adequately preserves each surviving requirement's original approval lineage and compliance-evidence chain

questions.question: An expert approval-legitimacy puzzle: MayOptimize requirements approved pre-acquisition by officers who have since departed (and whose roles no longer exist in the merged structure) are challenged by a Meridian architect: 'Approved by whom? questions.question: The remediation workstream needs a requirement change mid-audit-cycle: the regulator's examiners are ACTIVELY reviewing the current baseline while a genuine improvement to one committed requirement is identified. questions.question: Final KA5 stress case: two days before the remediation evidence submission, the BA's completeness check finds one committed requirement whose test evidence EXISTS but traces to a test run on the wrong environment (staging, not production — a genuine execution error, results likely identical but not provably so). options.A: Re-execute on production immediately if at all feasible within the window (the correct evidence may be 48 hours away — exhaust this first); if genuinely infeasible, submit with the discrepancy DISCLOSED: the requirement's evidence noted as staging-executed with production re-execution committed by a near date, rather than either silently including it (misrepresentation to a regulator — the maximum-severity integrity failure, and discoverable since environments are logged) or omitting the requirement entirely (a visible commitment gap inviting worse inferences than the disclosed truth). The ranking: correct evidence > disclosed imperfect evidence > gap > misrepresented evidence — with the last two orders of magnitude apart. Deadline pressure never reorders the top and bottom of that list
options.B: Simply omit the affected requirement from the evidence submission entirely, leaving no trace of it in the package and hoping the missing item goes unnoticed by the regulator's examiners within the larger submission, on the reasoning that removing the problematic item avoids both the misrepresentation risk of including mislabeled evidence and the discomfort of explicitly flagging a discrepancy, even though a submission that is supposed to cover every committed requirement but visibly omits one specific item creates its own conspicuous gap that examiners are likely to notice and may read even more unfavorably, on the further reasoning that a submission missing one item among many committed requirements might plausibly be read by examiners as an inadvertent clerical oversight rather than as a deliberate withholding, making silent omission seem like a lower-risk path than actively drawing attention to a specific, named evidentiary shortfall that examiners might not otherwise have noticed on their own within a large combined production
options.C: Relabel the staging-environment test results as though they had been executed against production, presenting the evidence package to the regulator as fully production-verified when the actual test run occurred on the wrong environment, on the reasoning that the staging and production environments are likely to have produced functionally identical results in this specific case, even though environments are independently logged in ways that make the true execution environment discoverable, and misrepresenting where a test actually ran to a regulator is a direct falsification of regulatory evidence
options.D: Submit the staging-environment test results as the requirement's evidence exactly as they currently exist, without disclosing that the execution occurred on the wrong environment, on the reasoning that the staging results are close enough in substance to what production execution would likely have shown, even though the regulator has no way of knowing the evidence was generated on the wrong environment unless the BA discloses it

questions.explanation:
A. ✓ Correct — re-execute on production if at all feasible within the window; if genuinely infeasible, submit with the discrepancy disclosed rather than omitted or misrepresented.

B. ✗ Omits the requirement entirely, creating a conspicuous, unexplained gap that a regulator may read even less favorably than an honestly disclosed and explained discrepancy would have been.

C. ✗ Relabels staging results as production, a direct falsification of regulatory evidence that's also discoverable through independent environment logs — the maximum-severity integrity failure on this list.

D. ✗ Submits the mislabeled evidence without disclosure, leaving the regulator unaware of a discrepancy that environment logs could independently reveal regardless of what the submission says.

options.D: Decline to raise the performance-fragility question with Meridian's strategic decision-makers at all, treating the acquisition's valuation methodology as exclusively Finance's domain and outside the BA's professional scope to comment on, on the reasoning that since Finance owns the formal valuation number, any BA-originated concern about what sustains the underlying performance that number is based on would be an inappropriate encroachment into a function that isn't the BA's to weigh in on

questions.question: An expert needs-analysis collision: Meridian's stated integration need is 'one platform, one process' (standardization economics); MayOptimize's claims performance partially DEPENDS on local adaptations (the branch-level flexibility, the assisted-submission channel for the 65+ segment). Standardization would eliminate adaptations that produce the performance being acquired. The strategic-analysis instrument for the standardization-versus-adaptation tension is:

options.A: Preserve every one of MayOptimize's existing local adaptations and branch-level variations exactly as they currently operate, resisting any standardization at all across the combined organization, on the reasoning that since the claims performance being acquired depends on local adaptation in at least some cases, the safest position is to assume all existing local variation is similarly value-producing and therefore worth protecting in its entirety, even though this treats cost-producing variation as equally worth preserving as the assisted-submission channel's demonstrated CSAT contribution, on the further reasoning that the specific, measured evidence separating value-producing adaptations from pure cost-producing drift may not yet exist in fully documented form for every branch-level variation across the estate, making blanket preservation the more cautious default until such evidence-gathering work can eventually be completed, rather than risking the standardization of some adaptation whose actual contribution to the acquired performance simply hasn't been measured and confirmed yet one way or the other
options.B: Let each individual branch vote on and decide for itself which of its own local process adaptations to keep or standardize away as part of the integration, on the reasoning that the people closest to each specific adaptation are best positioned to judge its value, even though branch-level votes would not be grounded in the same kind of measured-outcome evidence that actually distinguishes value-producing variation from pure historical drift
options.C: Decompose the estate by where variation creates versus destroys value: classify each local adaptation by its evidence — value-producing variation (the assisted channel's measured CSAT effect on its segment; adaptations with documented performance contribution) versus cost-producing variation (divergences with no outcome difference — pure historical drift, the standardization target) versus unexamined variation (requiring the outcome-comparison analysis before classification) — so the integration standardizes where variation is waste and preserves-as-designed-flexibility where variation is the performance mechanism (potentially EXPORTING the value-producing adaptations to Meridian's operations — the acquisition working backward). 'One process' as dogma destroys measured value; 'local everything' as dogma forfeits real synergies; the classification instrument replaces both dogmas with evidence
options.D: Standardize every one of MayOptimize's local adaptations onto Meridian's single, uniform process immediately as part of the integration, on the reasoning that synergy capture inherently requires full process uniformity across the combined organization, even though this would eliminate the assisted-submission channel's documented CSAT contribution to the 65+ segment along with every other measured, value-producing adaptation

questions.explanation:
A. ✗ Treats all local variation as equally worth preserving without distinguishing value-producing adaptations from pure historical drift, forfeiting real, achievable synergies the acquisition could otherwise capture.

B. ✗ Lets branch-level preference and local politics substitute for measured-outcome evidence, deciding what to keep or standardize on grounds unrelated to which adaptations actually produce measurable value.

C. ✓ Correct — classify each local adaptation by evidence (value-producing, cost-producing, or unexamined) so integration standardizes where variation is waste and preserves it where it's the performance mechanism.

D. ✗ Standardizes everything uniformly, eliminating the exact value-producing adaptations that the acquisition's own business case is valuing the operation for.

questions.question: The investigation's likely outcomes range from no-action to significant penalties with mandated oversight. Integration strategy must be set NOW, before the outcome is known. The expert strategy-under-unresolved-contingency design is:

options.B: Plan the entire integration strategy around the worst-case investigation outcome — significant penalties with mandated oversight — as the single assumption to build toward, on the reasoning that preparing for the most severe plausible scenario is the only safe posture, even though this commits organizational design and compliance-function decisions to a specific contingency before it's known to be the actual outcome
options.C: Structure the strategy around outcome-scenario branch points rather than a single assumed outcome: identify which integration decisions are OUTCOME-ROBUST (sensible under any investigation result — the semantic mapping, capability inventories, the remediation itself) and sequence them first; which are OUTCOME-CONTINGENT (organizational design and compliance-function decisions that mandated oversight would dictate differently — deferred past the expected resolution or designed with explicit adaptation points); and what each major outcome triggers (the pre-planned response per scenario, so resolution converts to execution rather than replanning crisis). questions.explanation:

B. ✗ Commits organizational and compliance decisions to the single worst-case branch before it's known to be the actual outcome, risking significant rework if the investigation concludes more favorably.

D. ✗ Commits organizational and compliance decisions to the single most favorable branch before it's known, leaving the integration unprepared under any less favorable outcome.

questions.question: An expert change-strategy paradox: integration requires MayOptimize staff to migrate to Meridian's platform — objectively a capability downgrade for claims handling in the near term (the gap analysis shows Meridian's platform lacks several DCMS capabilities until its enhancement roadmap delivers). Honest change communication would acknowledge the downgrade; morale and adoption require motivation. The expert communication-strategy resolution is:

A. ✗ Proposes an option the integration's own committed timeline doesn't actually accommodate, treating a discretionary preference as though it were an available choice within the real schedule constraints.

B. ✗ Tells staff a documented, concrete capability gap is merely their own perception, a claim their firsthand experience will directly contradict within days, at real cost to every future change message's credibility.

C. ✓ Correct — acknowledge the near-term gap explicitly, pair it with the committed remediation path and roadmap evidence, and create genuine agency in gap-priority sequencing and workaround design.

D. ✗ Omits the near-term gap in favor of the long-term vision, but staff discover the omitted gap firsthand within days regardless, adding a credibility problem on top of the capability gap itself.

questions.question: The expert gap-analysis reversal: standard integration gap analysis asks 'what does MayOptimize need that Meridian's platform lacks?' options.C: Treat any operational prerequisites Meridian's platform silently assumes but that MayOptimize's organization doesn't currently have in place as entirely Meridian's problem to solve rather than MayOptimize's transition scope to address, on the reasoning that since Meridian built and designed the platform around its own organization's existing operational structure, any mismatch is a platform design issue for Meridian to fix, rather than organizational-readiness work that the receiving organization needs to build, on the further reasoning that Meridian, as the platform's original designer and long-time operator, is better positioned to recognize and address whatever operational assumptions its own platform silently embeds than MayOptimize would be at identifying gaps in a system MayOptimize did not build and has no pre-existing operational familiarity with, making it reasonable to expect the platform's own home organization to carry primary responsibility for surfacing and resolving this particular category of mismatch
options.D: Conclude that no meaningful distinction exists between gaps identified in the forward direction and gaps identified in the reverse direction, treating all identified gaps as belonging to the same single remediation category and routing them all to the same owner and process, on the reasoning that from the receiving organization's perspective at go-live, any capability shortfall is simply a capability shortfall regardless of origin

questions.explanation:
A. ✓ Correct — the reverse analysis surfaces operating-assumption gaps: invisible organizational prerequisites the receiving organization must build to operate the platform, a class the forward analysis never surfaces.

B. ✗ Assumes the reverse analysis is redundant with the forward one, missing that it surfaces an entirely distinct risk class invisible to an analysis that only asks what the platform lacks.

C. ✗ Treats operating-assumption gaps as Meridian's problem to fix, when they're actually organizational-readiness work MayOptimize itself must build in order to operate the platform it's migrating onto.

D. ✗ Collapses forward and reverse gaps into one undifferentiated category, routing platform-enhancement work and organizational-readiness work to the same owner instead of their genuinely different remediation paths.

questions.question: An expert prioritization-authority collapse: mid-integration, the designated prioritization authority (Meridian's platform PO) is reassigned with no successor for 6 weeks, while prioritization decisions queue. The interim options each have defects: the lead BA deciding (authority overreach), the queue waiting (delivery stall), stakeholder consensus per item (slow, gameable). The expert interim design is:

options.B: Have the lead BA personally make every prioritization decision that arises during the 6-week authority gap, reasoning that someone has to keep decisions flowing and delivery moving during the interim period, and that the BA's proximity to the requirements and stakeholders makes them the most practical person to step into the vacant decision role temporarily, even though prioritization — including value-trading and irreversible calls — is specifically the authority that belongs to the platform PO role and not to the BA function

questions.explanation:

B. ✗ Has the BA personally exercise prioritization authority — including irreversible, value-trading calls — that specifically belongs to the PO role, exactly the overreach a bounded interim design is meant to avoid.

C. ✓ Correct — partition by reversibility: mechanical published rules for reversible sequencing calls now, queued escalation with impact-of-delay documented for irreversible ones, with successor reversal authority over everything decided interim.

D. ✗ Applies slow, per-item stakeholder voting to every decision including reversible sequencing calls, and is vulnerable to whichever stakeholders show up in force gaming any given vote's outcome.

questions.question: A change-request pattern analysis across the integration reveals: 60% of CRs originate from the semantic mapping's ongoing corrections (false-friend discoveries rippling into requirements). Each is processed individually through full change control. The expert process-adaptation for high-volume systematic change is:

The monitoring layer: if a 'mapping correction' batch item shows anomalous impact (touching requirements beyond the mapping's ripple pattern), it ejects to individual processing — class-based channels need class-membership verification or they become bypass routes. options.B: Halt further corrections to the semantic mapping table in order to reduce the volume of change requests flowing through change control, on the reasoning that since 60% of CRs originate from ongoing mapping corrections, simply stopping that correction work is the most direct way to bring the CR volume down to a more manageable level, even though the underlying mapping corrections are addressing real false-friend discoveries that, if left uncorrected, would leave requirements built on definitional errors the earlier semantic-bridge analysis specifically identified as high-risk

questions.explanation:
A. ✓ Correct — create a class-based batch channel for mapping-correction changes with consolidated review and an anomaly-ejection rule, since class-based channels need class-membership verification or they become bypass routes.

B. ✗ Stops correcting real, high-risk false-friend discoveries just to reduce the visible CR count, removing governance and correction from the highest-value change source instead of scaling how it's processed.

C. ✗ Removes all governance oversight rather than consolidating it into class-based batch review, leaving anomalous, out-of-pattern mapping changes with no mechanism to catch them before they land.

questions.question: An expert approval-evidence question for the monitorship era: the compliance monitor asks not whether requirements were approved, but 'how does the organization know its approvers actually engage with what they sign?' The evidence of approval SUBSTANCE (beyond process compliance) that a mature organization can produce is:

options.A: Behavioral traces of engagement: correction rates in approval cycles (approvers who periodically reject, amend, or question demonstrate engagement — a 100% frictionless approval rate is the hollow-signature signature), documented approval-stage findings (the Legal Officer's conditional approval with the DPA condition; the PO's section-3.4 doubts surfaced and resolved), reviewer questions on record, and version deltas between submitted and approved (evidence the review changed things) — because engagement leaves marks, and an approval history with zero marks across hundreds of decisions evidences ceremony, not scrutiny. The organization that tracked its 100%-CCB-approval anomaly and its hollow-signature incident can show the monitor its own detection of engagement failure — which is the maturity evidence itself
options.B: Have approvers across the organization sign sworn statements formally attesting that they personally read and considered every document they have ever approved, on the reasoning that a sworn, formal attestation of engagement carries significant evidentiary weight, even though a sworn statement is itself just another signature-style assertion rather than behavioral evidence, and can be produced with equal ease by an approver who genuinely reads everything and one who has never meaningfully engaged with a single document
options.C: Extend the length of approval review meetings and maintain detailed attendance logs showing who was present for how long during each approval cycle, on the reasoning that longer meetings with documented attendance demonstrate a visible, recordable commitment of time the monitor can point to as evidence of engagement, even though time spent in a room and attendance at a meeting measure presence and duration rather than the actual substantive engagement that distinguishes genuine scrutiny from someone simply sitting through a longer meeting
options.D: Produce signature timestamps and system logs proving that approvers technically opened each document before affixing their electronic signature, on the reasoning that a verifiable, timestamped record showing a document was opened prior to signature demonstrates the approver at least had the opportunity to review the content, even though opening a document and actually engaging with its substance are different things entirely, and a timestamp provides no information about whether anything in it was actually read, questioned, or influenced the decision, on the further reasoning that a timestamp is at least an objective, machine-generated data point rather than a subjective human account of engagement, making it seem like harder, more defensible evidence to present to a skeptical monitor even though it measures nothing about whether the document's actual content shaped the approver's ultimate decision in any way

questions.explanation:
A. ✓ Correct — evidence engagement through behavioral traces: correction rates, documented approval-stage findings, reviewer questions on record, and version deltas between submitted and approved text.

B. ✗ Offers another signature-style assertion rather than behavioral evidence — a sworn statement can be produced identically by an engaged and a disengaged approver alike, giving the monitor no way to distinguish the two.

C. ✗ Measures time and presence rather than substantive engagement — a longer meeting with full attendance says nothing about whether anyone actually questioned, corrected, or changed anything.

D. ✗ Proves a document was technically opened, which says nothing about whether its content was actually read, questioned, or influenced the approver's decision.

questions.question: The integration's hardest tracing case: a Meridian platform capability will satisfy 14 MayOptimize requirements 'in aggregate' — no one-to-one mapping exists because the platform solves the underlying problem differently (its unified workflow replaces the 14 requirements' separate mechanisms). The traceability and validation treatment of many-to-one-via-different-mechanism satisfaction is:

options.A: Aggregate satisfaction requires NEED-level validation, not requirement-level mapping: the 14 requirements were mechanisms serving needs — the platform's different mechanism must be validated against the NEEDS (elevating the trace: requirement → underlying need → platform capability, with the need layer made explicit where it was previously implicit), tested by the scenario method against the needs' acceptance evidence (do the 14 requirements' original validation scenarios pass under the unified workflow?), and examined for residue (mechanisms sometimes served secondary needs invisibly — the displaced co-product lesson: does any of the 14 carry a function the unified workflow drops?). 'Satisfied differently' is a transformation claim requiring the equivalence discipline at need level — the mapping alone (A) records a conclusion no one has tested
options.B: Rewrite all 14 of the original MayOptimize requirements so their text directly describes Meridian's unified workflow mechanism instead of describing the original 14 separate mechanisms they were written against, on the reasoning that updating the requirement text to match the platform's actual implementation resolves the tracing mismatch cleanly, even though this reverses the proper direction of specification — requirements exist to describe the underlying business need, not to describe whatever mechanism a particular solution happens to implement
options.C: Reject Meridian's platform capability as unsuitable because its unified workflow mechanism doesn't match the 14 separate mechanisms the original requirements describe, on the reasoning that a capability satisfying the underlying needs through a materially different mechanism represents a mismatch serious enough to disqualify the capability entirely, even though the actual test of suitability is whether the platform's different mechanism satisfies the needs the 14 requirements originally existed to serve, which a mechanism-level text comparison alone cannot determine, on the further reasoning that requiring a materially different mechanism to nonetheless prove its equivalence at the level of underlying needs adds analytical work that could be avoided entirely simply by insisting from the outset that any accepted capability must replicate the original 14 mechanisms closely enough to satisfy a straightforward mechanism-level comparison
options.D: Map all 14 requirements to the single Meridian platform capability and mark each one satisfied in the traceability matrix without any further testing, on the reasoning that once a many-to-one correspondence has been established and recorded, the disposition is complete and no additional validation work is needed, even though 'satisfied differently' is fundamentally a transformation claim that a mapping link alone records as a conclusion without anyone having actually tested whether it's true

questions.explanation:
A. ✓ Correct — validate at the need level: elevate the trace to requirement → need → capability, test the unified workflow against the 14 requirements' original validation scenarios, and check for dropped secondary functions.

B. ✗ Reverses the proper direction of specification, rewriting requirements around the incumbent platform's mechanism instead of keeping them anchored to the underlying need — a rewrite that would need undoing again under any future different mechanism.

C. ✗ Confuses mechanism difference with need failure, rejecting a capability that might fully satisfy the underlying needs simply because its mechanism doesn't textually match the original requirements' mechanism-level descriptions.

D. ✗ Records a mapping conclusion without testing it, treating 'satisfied differently' as though it were self-evidently true rather than a transformation claim requiring need-level scenario validation.

questions.question: An expert records-lifecycle boundary: the investigation closes (moderate penalty, monitor installed). Counsel releases the litigation hold. The BA must now decide the disposition of the held materials — including candid internal analyses whose retention beyond legal minimums carries discovery risk in hypothetical FUTURE litigation, but whose content documents the remediation's rationale. options.A: Disposition by the organization's retention policy applied honestly — not by litigation-fear minimization or packrat maximalism: the retention schedule (designed with counsel, balancing operational value, compliance obligations, and litigation exposure as a POLICY matter) governs — materials within their retention periods stay; expired materials route through normal disposition; and the remediation-rationale documents likely have AFFIRMATIVE retention value (the monitor's tenure makes the remediation's evidence chain operationally live for 3 more years, and the decision-history's value was established repeatedly). options.D: Delete every document that was under the litigation hold immediately once counsel formally releases the hold, regardless of each document's individual retention-period status or ongoing operational and evidentiary value, on the reasoning that removing everything immediately upon release minimizes any lingering discovery exposure as completely and quickly as possible, even though the remediation-rationale documents specifically retain real, affirmative operational value for the 3-year duration of the monitor's own tenure

questions.explanation:

questions.question: A cross-organizational baseline dispute with money attached: Meridian claims a migration deliverable is complete per the agreed baseline; MayOptimize operations claims the delivered capability omits committed behavior. questions.question: An expert environmental-shift case: mid-integration, a major insurtech enters the market with AI-native claims processing, and Meridian's board asks whether the integration's target platform is 'already obsolete.' questions.question: An expert validation-audience problem: appeals-process requirements need validation, and the monitorship means the DESIGN will eventually be assessed against fairness standards by the monitor. questions.question: A requirements-architecture question at merger scale: the combined estate (post-rationalization) spans 900+ requirements across two heritage structures, three initiatives, and the monitor's control framework. questions.question: An expert recommendation-integrity case: the lead BA's analysis supports migrating the fraud module LAST (its DCMS implementation outperforms Meridian's roadmap equivalent for 18+ months), but the BA knows this recommendation extends the BA team's own relevance and headcount — a conflict of interest that doesn't make the analysis wrong.
